File Photo by Marie Jeanne Munyyerenkana/EPA Aug. 16 (UPI) -- The ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo became the nation's deadliest over the weekend with a death toll of more than 2,300, according to local health officials. The DRC's public health institute on Sunday reported 2,325 Ebola deaths since the first cases were reported in late April, surpassing the previous record of 2,299 deaths during the 2018-2020 outbreak. "Ebola is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo," Tom Fletcher, United Nations under-secretary general for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, said in a Friday statement. "We cannot let the virus outrun our response." The DRC declared the outbreak, the nation's 17th since the disease was first discovered in 1976, on May 15, when there were 246 suspected cases, eight laboratory-confirmed cases and 80 deaths. On April 24, the first suspect case, a healthcare worker, developed Ebola symptoms of fever, hemorrhaging, vomiting and intense malaise, and later died. Local health officials on Sunday reported a total of 4,945 confirmed cases. Ebola is often fatal with a mortality rate of around 50%, according to the World Health Organization. It is transmitted to people from wild animals and spreads through direct contact with blood and other bodily fluids of infected individuals. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a severe form of Ebola that WHO officials said is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be its natural reservoir. Infection occurs through close contact with blood or secretions of infected wildlife. There are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for Bundibugyo, meaning outbreak control methods include rapid case identification, contact tracing, isolation and care, safe burials and strong community engagement. Despite mitigation efforts, the virus appears to be aggressively spreading. The WHO on Friday said there had been 579 cases and 304 deaths during the Aug. 3-9 week, the highest weekly numbers reported of the outbreak, "The ongoing humanitarian crisis, compounded by insecurity, population displacement and mobility and cross-border movements continues to pose significant challenges to response efforts and increase the risk of further geographical spread," the WHO said in its update. According to Fletcher, the outbreak is the fastest-growing on record, resulting in a death every 30 minutes. "We need to double the number of teams ensuring safe and dignified burials, triple the treatment capacity, improve contact tracing and deploy more experienced managers," he said. "Crucially, we must meet the immense needs for water, hygiene, healthcare and other basic services in the region." Uganda, which reported an outbreak after infected individuals crossed into the country from DRC, declared itself Ebola-free late last month. content: Skip to main content Global editionTuesday, August 18, 2026 Streamline Search⌘KWriteSign inJoin Streamline StreamlineGlobal edition LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSportDirectoryHouse HuntingPeopleHistoryMore LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSport Back to News/Health Health WHO Tests Cross-Protection Of Zaire Ebola Vaccine Against New Strains The World Health Organization is evaluating whether the licensed Zaire ebolavirus vaccine can offer cross-protection against the Sudan and Bundibugyo strains amid rising outbreak concerns in East Africa. Streamline Feed OfficialVerified Aug 18, 2026Updated Aug 18, 20263 min read Follow on Google News Try askingGive me the 30-second brief Sponsored Novus Consult 9s Article Learn more Current storyWHO Tests Cross-Protection Of Zaire Ebola Vaccine Against New Strains Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Global health authorities are racing against time to determine if a vaccine designed for one strain of Ebola can shield populations from entirely different variants of the deadly hemorrhagic fever. The World Health Organization (WHO) is preparing to test the cross-protective efficacy of Merck's Ervebo vaccine, currently licensed solely for the Zaire ebolavirus, against the Sudan and Bundibugyo strains that have recently triggered outbreaks in East and Central Africa, potentially rewriting the playbook for epidemic response. The Science of Cross-Protection Ebola virus disease is not a monolith; it is caused by several distinct species within the Ebolavirus genus, with Zaire, Sudan, and Bundibugyo being the most lethal to humans. Ervebo, the only FDA and EMA-approved Ebola vaccine, was developed specifically to target the glycoprotein of the Zaire ebolavirus, which was responsible for the devastating 2014-2016 West African epidemic. However, immunological data suggests that the immune response generated by Ervebo might offer partial, albeit unquantified, protection against other species due to structural similarities in the viral envelope. Scientists at the WHO's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) on Immunization are currently reviewing pre-clinical data and limited human serological studies to determine if deploying Ervebo during a Sudan or Bundibugyo outbreak could reduce transmission rates and mortality. The stakes are extraordinarily high; the Sudan ebolavirus, which recently ravaged parts of Uganda, has a case fatality rate of up to 50 percent, and there are currently no licensed vaccines or targeted therapeutics available for it. If Ervebo can provide even a 30 percent cross-protection rate, it could be deployed as a stopgap measure to protect frontline healthcare workers and ring-vaccinate affected communities while strain-specific vaccines undergo clinical trials. Clinical Trials and Regulatory Hurdles Testing a licensed vaccine for an off-label indication during an active outbreak presents immense logistical and ethical challenges. The WHO is coordinating with national regulatory authorities in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo to design adaptive clinical trial protocols. These trials will measure neutralizing antibody titers in individuals who receive Ervebo during a non-Zaire outbreak, comparing their outcomes against historical control groups. Regulatory bodies must balance the urgent need for intervention with the imperative to gather robust efficacy data, ensuring that public trust in vaccination campaigns is not undermined by unproven interventions. Furthermore, the global stockpile of Ervebo is finite, managed by the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision. Diverting doses to combat a strain it was not explicitly designed for could leave populations vulnerable to a resurgence of the Zaire strain. This necessitates a complex risk-benefit analysis, weighing the immediate threat of the current outbreak against the latent risk of a Zaire re-emergence. East African Preparedness and Kenyan Defenses For Kenya, the WHO's cross-protection evaluation is of paramount strategic importance. Although Kenya has never recorded a domestic Ebola outbreak, its position as a regional transit hub makes it highly vulnerable to imported cases. The Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) has been at the forefront of regional genomic surveillance, sequencing viral samples from neighboring countries to track strain mutations. The Kenya Ministry of Health maintains strict screening protocols at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport and the porous borders with Uganda and South Sudan. If the WHO validates Ervebo's cross-protective efficacy, Kenya's national pandemic preparedness framework will immediately integrate the vaccine into its emergency response arsenal. The Epidemiological Surveillance unit in Nairobi is already modeling deployment scenarios, ensuring that cold-chain logistics are optimized to handle the rapid distribution of the vaccine to border counties like Busia and Mandera. The outcome of these trials will not only dictate the response to the current outbreaks but will fundamentally reshape how the African continent prepares for the inevitable emergence of novel filoviruses, proving that scientific agility is the ultimate defense against epidemic threats. The largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded was a 2014-16 outbreak in West Africa, which killed 11,325 over two years. The current outbreak is moving at a faster pace than that outbreak, however, and with no effective vaccine or therapeutics against the Bundibugyo strain, experts warn it could become the world’s deadliest in a matter of months. There have been almost 5,000 cases recorded in three months, meaning the case-fatality rate (CFR) is now hovering around 46%. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), CFRs in the past two Bundibugyo outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively. Late last week, United Nations (UN) humanitarian affairs chief Tom Fletcher said that, due to the high CFR, he has allocated an additional $30.5 million from the UN’s Central Emergency Response Fund to fight the outbreak. The money is in addition to the $24 million previously allocated to the DRC and neighboring countries for this outbreak. This is a wake-up call. “This is a wake-up call,” Fletcher said. “We need speed, scale and solidarity before this virus gets even further ahead of us.” No signs of abating In the latest Disease Outbreak News update from the WHO, the agency said the outbreak was showing no signs of abating. “During the most recent reporting week (epidemiological week 32, 3 to 9 August 2026), the highest weekly number of reported cases (579) and deaths (304) were recorded, highlighting the exceptional pace of transmission,” the WHO said. As of August 12, 100 new cases were being recorded every 24 hours. Infections among health workers continue, the WHO said. with at least 155 confirmed cases, including 45 deaths (CFR, 29%) and 68 recoveries since beginning of the outbreak. Tomorrow, the International Health Regulations Emergency Committee will hold its second meeting since May regarding the outbreak. (AP Photo/Dieudonne Dirole) By Associated Press PUBLISHED: August 13, 2026 at 10:23 AM EDT | UPDATED: August 13, 2026 at 1:25 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... KINSHASA, Congo (AP) — Congo’s Ebola outbreak has spread to a sixth province after a death was recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province, the head of Africa’s CDC said Thursday. The man died in Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, after traveling there from Isiro in Haut-Uele province, said Jean Kaseya, director general of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. The outbreak in eastern Congo, considered the fastest-growing one yet, is on track to surpass the deadliest one in history, which erupted over a decade ago and killed over 11,000 people, the World Health Organization said Wednesday. There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo virus responsible for the current outbreak. It has killed over 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures. This death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 Ebola outbreak in West Africa — the worst in history. The outbreak is unfolding in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable, with strikes by some unpaid health workers, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatized communities and misinformation asserting that Ebola isn’t real. Bas-Uele is a vast province in northeastern Congo that borders the Central African Republic, where there is recurring armed violence that has forced thousands to flee and take refuge in the province. Access can be difficult due to bad and poorly connected roads as well as limited communication networks, and there are frequent population movements related to gold mining and displacement from conflict. As of Thursday, six out of 26 of Congo’s provinces have been impacted. About 90% of all cases and 80% of deaths are concentrated in Ituri province, the WHO said Wednesday. Mercy Corps, an aid group, warned Thursday that Ebola cases have been reported along a major travel route about 35 kilometers (22 miles) from Congo’s border with South Sudan, expressing concern over the outbreak’s “widening footprint.” No cases have been confirmed in South Sudan so far. (AP Photo/Dieudonne Dirole) A health worker dries boots that were washed to prevent the spread of the Ebola virus at the treatment centre in Bunia General Hospital in Ituri, eastern Congo, Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Dieudonne Dirole) Health workers tend to an Ebola patient at the Rwampara Treatment Center in Ituri, Congo, Thursday, June 18, 2026. (AP Photo/Dieudonne Dirole) Expand Unpaid health workers strikes and low contact tracing hamper response Meanwhile, health workers at the Nizi Treatment Center in Ituri province, one of the most affected in the area, went on strike Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the center after they said they have not been paid for three months. Kaseya on Thursday called on the Congolese government to pay the outstanding salaries. “We need to pay health workers,” he told reporters. “This is the responsibility of the government, not partners. And they told us that money is available.” The real scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on May 15, but the WHO now says sequencing showed it began months earlier, in February. Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an “alarming” rate. Contact tracing helps break chains of transmission by finding exposed people early and reacting quickly if they show symptoms. “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us,” the WHO regional director for Africa, Dr. Mohamed Yakub Janabi, said this week. On Thursday, Kaseya from Africa CDC said “the concept of contact tracing in DRC has become useless.” Trials for treatments and vaccines are underway Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal. Clinical trials of two possible treatments for this type of Ebola began last month in Ituri, the most affected of the five provinces in Congo where cases have been reported. Two vaccines developed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus are now being tested in people for the first time, the WHO said Wednesday. WHO also plans to test whether an existing Ebola vaccine could protect people against the virus after studies in animals showed promising results. Kaseya said on Thursday that Africa CDC supports the use of Ervebo, a vaccine authorized against the Zaire Ebola strain in provinces impacted by Bundibugyo virus. He said some studies show some cross-protection from the available vaccines. “We are in a gray area,” he said. “And when you are in a gray area, you have to make strong decisions to stop seeing people dying.” Associated Press reporters Constant Same Bagalwa in Bunia, Congo and Justin Kabumba in Goma, Congo contributed. Report now Democratic Republic of the Congo There are already more than 5,000 confirmed cases of Ebola in the Congo ARCHIVE – ARCHIVE. A healthcare worker sprays disinfectant at the Ebola treatment center at the General Hospital in eastern Congo. More than 2,300 people have died from the viral disease so far. Photo: Dieudonne Dirole/AP/dpa Keystone More than 5,000 cases of Ebola have now been confirmed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. According to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Regional Office for Africa, 5,021 people have been confirmed to have contracted the highly contagious infectious disease since May. To date, 2,378 patients have died from Ebola in this Central African country—a case fatality rate of 47.4 percent. Still, according to Congolese health authorities, more than 1,000 patients are considered to have recovered. The outbreak was announced in mid-May. This marks the 17th time Ebola has occurred in the country. Keystone-SDA Today at 16:52 The number of Ebola cases could be even higher However, the African Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has already pointed out that the actual number of cases could be even higher. Studies suggest that the outbreak began around February, emphasized Jean Kaseya, the agency’s director, in his latest report on the situation. “We have no idea what happened between February and May.” All data on case numbers cover only the period from May to the present. “We are not claiming that this data is accurate,” Kaseya said. Furthermore, nearly two-thirds of confirmed Ebola deaths are not recorded in hospitals and isolation wards, but in villages and communities. As long as patients with symptoms are not isolated, they can transmit the disease through contact with bodily fluids such as blood, sweat, or saliva—for example, when washing a patient or eating. Weeks ago, Africa CDC had already warned that not all cases of the disease might be reported to the authorities. Life-Threatening Fever Ebola is a life-threatening disease. The virus is transmitted through physical contact and contact with bodily fluids, and causes a highly contagious fever accompanied by diarrhea and bleeding. The current outbreak is particularly difficult to contain, in part because there is currently neither a specific vaccine nor a specific treatment for the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus. Clinical trials of two antiviral treatments have been underway since early July. Given the severity of the outbreak, researchers are also investigating whether the virus may have mutated. The largest outbreak ever recorded? The World Health Organization also fears that the current outbreak in the Congo could reach unprecedented proportions. Already, the number of cases and deaths is several times higher than during the most severe outbreak to date in West Africa over a comparable three-month period.
